name: Fadogia agrestis
lead: Fadogia agrestis (now often classified as Vangueria agrestis) is a plant of the coffee family, Rubiaceae, native to tropical Africa. Its stem has been used in traditional African medicine as an aphrodisiac and for pain and inflammation, and extracts are sold as dietary supplements marketed for testosterone and libido.[1][3][2]

The research is almost entirely in rodents. A 2005 study in male rats reported higher serum testosterone and more sexual behaviour after dosing with an aqueous stem extract, and a 2023 rat study reported effects on erectile-dysfunction biomarkers.[3][4] Rat studies have also examined testicular function and liver and kidney toxicity.[5][6] No human clinical trial of Fadogia agrestis was found in the sources reviewed.
In forums and on podcasts it is often combined with tongkat ali in 'natural testosterone' stacks, and the combination is discussed alongside concerns drawn from the animal toxicity studies.[7][8]
infobox: Tropical Africa (the genus ranges from West to East and southern Africa)[1]

paras: Fadogia is a genus of more than 100 perennial herbs, subshrubs and shrubs in the family Rubiaceae, found in savanna and woodland across tropical and southern Africa. Fadogia agrestis has been transferred by some taxonomists to Vangueria, which is how it appears in some chemical literature.[1][9] Phytochemical work has identified alkaloids and saponins in stem extracts, and separate studies isolated monoterpene glycosides and ursane-type triterpenoid glycosides, benzophenone glycosides and an iridoid glucoside from the plant.[3][9][10]

A survey of Ghana's herbal markets found that plants sold there were mostly used for women's health, rituals, as aphrodisiacs and against sexually transmitted diseases, illustrating the context of traditional aphrodisiac plant use in West Africa, though it does not specifically document Fadogia.[11]

Traditionally, Fadogia agrestis is described as being used in African medicine for its analgesic, anti-inflammatory and aphrodisiac activities.[2] Today, supplements claiming to contain it are sold for testosterone support and libido. A 2019 analytical study of 17 dietary supplements claiming to contain F. agrestis found that 12 contained measurable phenolic compounds at low levels and 5 did not, indicating variability in products.[2]

subs.h: Animal studies of testosterone and sexual behaviour
paras: In the 2005 study, male albino rats were given an aqueous stem extract at 18, 50 and 100 mg/kg for several days; all doses increased mount and intromission frequency, prolonged ejaculatory latency and increased serum testosterone, with the authors suggesting the testosterone rise might underlie the aphrodisiac effect.[3] A 2023 study in paroxetine-treated rats found that the extract raised nitric oxide, cGMP and antioxidant enzymes and lowered PDE5 and other markers in penile and testicular tissue, in a pattern the authors compared to sildenafil.[4]

A 2008 study examined testicular function indices in male rats given the aqueous stem extract and followed recovery for ten days.[5] A 2009 study examined the mode of cellular toxicity of the extract in rat liver and kidney.[6] The abstracts available to this wiki do not report full results, and no regulatory body safety assessment was found.

Separately, other species in the genus and related genera, including Fadogia homblei, Pavetta and Vangueria, are associated with gousiekte, a fatal cardiotoxicosis of ruminants in South Africa; this is a veterinary phenomenon of different plants and has not been shown to apply to supplement use in humans.[12][1]

Fadogia agrestis became widely known through podcasts and social media as a testosterone-support supplement, usually paired with tongkat ali. On T Nation, users describe taking it with tongkat ali for energy and libido, adding it to 'HPTA restart' and post-cycle routines, or trying it after concerns about testicular size; one poster credits a podcaster's recommendation as 'right', while another reported that SHBG did not change after trying boron, Fadogia and tongkat ali.[7][8][13][14]
Users commonly describe cycling the supplement on and off; this wiki does not give dosing or cycling instructions.

No studies found. Research is limited to rodent studies of aphrodisiac effects, testicular function and organ toxicity,[3][4][5][6] chemical analyses of the plant and supplements,[2][9][10] and veterinary literature on related plants.[12]

lore.intro: Fadogia agrestis is discussed on T Nation as one half of a tongkat ali plus Fadogia 'natural test' stack, often used when trying to restart or support testosterone, with anecdotes ranging from praise to no measurable change.[7][8][13][14]

claims.claim: Fadogia agrestis raises testosterone in men
claims.believers: A T Nation user says the tongkat ali and Fadogia combination helps 'energy and libido' and credits a podcaster's recommendation.[7] Others add it to restart routines.[13]
claims.experts: Evidence for raised testosterone comes from a 2005 rat study; no human trial has tested it.[3]

claims.claim: Fadogia can help restore testicular function or recovery after steroid or hormone use
claims.believers: T Nation posters mention taking it for a few weeks after HCG therapy or hoping it helps recovery from testicular shrinkage.[15][16]
claims.experts: A rat study examined testicular function indices after extract dosing; no human studies on testicular recovery were found.[5]

claims.claim: Fadogia is safe at supplement doses
claims.believers: Users describe it as a low-risk option and use it regularly, usually cycling it.[7][14]
claims.experts: Rat studies have examined toxicity in liver and kidney and testicular indices, and related plants cause cardiac toxicity in ruminants; no human safety trials exist.[5][6][12]

claims.claim: Stacking Fadogia with tongkat ali is synergistic
claims.believers: Users commonly combine the two for libido and energy and recommend vendors with care about product quality.[7][13]
claims.experts: No published trial has tested the combination; a 2019 analysis found variable phenolic content across supplements claiming to contain Fadogia.[2]

card.summary: Podcast-famous African stem extract sold as a testosterone booster; supported only by rat studies, with toxicity questions unanswered in humans.
card.note: No human trials; rat studies include testicular and liver/kidney toxicity work, and supplement content varies.

quick.overview:
Fadogia agrestis is an African plant whose stem extract is sold as a testosterone and libido supplement, usually alongside tongkat ali. It became widely known through podcasts and fitness social media.

Almost all evidence is from rats, including a 2005 study reporting higher serum testosterone and more mating behaviour. No human clinical trial was found.
quick.mechanism: In rodents, extracts raised serum testosterone and, in a rat erectile model, shifted nitric oxide pathway markers; the mechanism in humans has not been studied.
quick.risks: Rat studies have looked at testicular function and liver and kidney toxicity, and related plant species cause cardiac toxicity in livestock. Human safety data do not exist, and a 2019 analysis found supplement contents differ widely.
